🇩🇪 Germany has lost nearly 500,000 industrial jobs since 2019 according to an Ifo ​study. Yet the country continues to create jobs and that is where the real problem with the German economy lies.

📊 Including certain estimates for temporary workers, the losses could reach 628,000 jobs but all these losses are concentrated in the sectors that have historically driven Germany's industrial strength. We are talking about 123,500 jobs lost in the automotive industry and its suppliers, 115,600 in fabricated metal products, and 64,500 in machinery manufacturing. Together, these three sectors account for 60% of all industrial job losses.

⚠️ Over the same period, the country added approximately 1.7 million jobs overall, largely driven by the services sector, which gained more than 2.2 million jobs. However, a significant share of this job creation has been concentrated in public administration, healthcare, education, and social services. These activities are essential but they do not offer the same potential for productivity gains, innovation, and exports as Germany's traditional industrial sectors.

➡️ To understand this transformation, we need to look at the foundations of Germany's economic model. For decades, its success relied on high-end manufacturing, highly specialized exporting companies, a skilled workforce, relatively competitive energy costs, and strong international demand. Today, these advantages are being challenged as energy costs remain elevated, demographic aging is increasing labor market pressures, and international competition is intensifying. I am afraid of the emergence of a vicious cycle as weakening competitiveness could discourage investment, slow innovation, and further undermine the country's productive capacity. Moreover, this transformation is taking place at a time when demographic aging is increasing the financial burden of pensions, healthcare, and long-term care.

Germany appears to be gradually losing some of the economic advantages that made it so successful, and without a recovery in competitiveness, what currently looks like an industrial crisis could turn into a lasting crisis of Germany's entire growth model.

@base has led @solana in DeFi TVL for 10 straight days, the first time since 2023.

But it's not as big a deal as it sounds. Here's why:

• Base's lead comes from one app. @Morpho holds ~$4.4B of Base's $6.16B, and ~97% of Base's growth over the last 30 days ($258M of $265M) went into it.

• Solana didn't really lose money. Its TVL is down ~7%, and SOL's price is down ~6%. The tokens are still there, they're just worth less.

• Solana still holds ~3x more stablecoins ($15.8B vs $5.1B on Base). Most of it just isn't deposited in DeFi apps, so TVL doesn't count it.

So if Morpho has a bad week, Base loses its lead. And if SOL's price goes back up, Solana could take the spot back without anyone moving a dollar.

If you're earning yield on Base, check who runs your Morpho vault and how much of the yield comes from token rewards.

Next time you see a chain ranking, ask two questions. Did TVL just follow the token price? Is one app doing all the work?

I don't envy the position of trying to solve this, but I will say:
1. It is a positive, however hard you have to skew to see it, that they are acting quickly on closing down attack vectors - this should be priority no.1 and with a non-transferable token, the second part can be worked out in time. If you reverse the order, there is nothing left to be saved
2. Whilst the token remains non-transferrable there is still time for the team and community to iterate on this and work out a better/more balanced path forward and I hope people do come forward with ideas
3. As far as I can tell the team are smart, but also willing to listen to others and suggestions to improve, and I believe in an ideal world they want a solution that balances protecting the protocol as well as rewarding users, so if that can be found - I do believe they'd listen

However, for now, this is a pretty disappointing update and think the sustainability of a protocol depends both on its technical risk and social risk (obviously with 1 being more black and white than the other). So whilst this is understandable, in its current form, it is incredibly damaging to the social risk of papertrade and believe it probably won't survive in the meaningful way people had hoped, without further iteration on this model

Overall, Disappointed, but hopeful a better solution can be found in time, and the non-transferability gives time for that solution to be found. Best of luck to the team and users

I know it sounds cliche but IRL really is the alpha.

Mudwater was stressful ngl. There was a lot to get into place right up until the last minute but we fucking did it and I'm so proud of the team and the work we put in.

clubhouse and anime are still coming btw, I know people wanted announcements or a keynote or whatever but sometimes the timing doesn't line up with apefest. That doesn't mean Yuga forgot or abandoned those plans.

Sometimes it's just about getting everybody together and having a good time.

I love that shit. Every year, seeing old friends and making new ones. Finally putting faces to names.

This club is special. I say it every year but  we are in such a unique position to have connections all over the world that share this common interest.

If you're an ape, you have a friend in every city on earth. One in every hobby and every industry. It's hard to describe how unique and special our weird little group of internet jpeg collectors is.

I don't really know what the point of this post is other than to say I'm so thankful for the club and for everybody I met and didn't get to meet this weekend. So many people I wish I could've spent some time with, or more time with. Just know you're all always welcome in my part of the world. If you need a couch, or dinner recs, or a good cup of coffee, let's fucking do it. we don't need to wait for apefest every year.

I give my everything to this space because it's given everything to me. Y'all will always be family.

Bored Apes Forever.
